subject: VAPA
overview: VAPA 2 moves through units on line and shape, rhythm, color, melody, texture and form, instruments, world art, movement and drama, and ends with a home showcase; plan on about 30 minutes a day. Each week: look at or listen to a real work first ('I see… I think… I wonder…'), model the skill briefly, let your child create, then have them reflect using the week's vocabulary. Pull up artwork images from museum websites and recordings before the week starts, keep everything in a dated portfolio and sketchbook for weeks 32-36, and praise thoughtful choices more than 'realistic' results.

weeks.prep: New sketchbook, pencils, markers, crayons, a few pieces of yarn; calm and energetic music clips. Set up a cleanup routine (caps on, tools back in bin, wipe table).
misconceptions: Thinking a line must be straight or drawn with a ruler: lines can be curved, zigzag, wavy, spiral, dotted, thick or thin.
Thinking a contour line is just the outside 'scribble': a contour line carefully follows the edge of a shape.

days.guide: Walk inside and outside hunting lines (fence = vertical/straight, branches = curved/diagonal, stairs = zigzag). Sketch each of 10 lines in the new sketchbook.

questions.q: What kind of line does a staircase make from the side?
questions.a: Zigzag (step-like) lines.

questions.q: What kind of lines are fence posts?
questions.a: Straight vertical lines.

days.guide: Fold paper into 12 boxes; fill each with a different line using markers and label it.

questions.a: A line that curls around a center point, getting bigger or smaller.
A line that follows the outside edge of an object.

days.guide: Play calm music and draw lines to match, then energetic music. Discuss: calm = long, wavy, horizontal; excited = zigzag, short, jagged. Practice cleanup.

questions.q: What kind of line feels calm?
questions.a: Smooth, wavy or horizontal lines.

questions.q: What kind of line feels excited?
questions.a: Zigzag, jagged or short quick lines.

days.guide: Drop yarn on paper, trace its shape, and turn it into an imaginative drawing.

questions.q: What did your yarn line become?
questions.a: Child describes their drawing.

days.guide: Share the sampler; name a favorite line using words like zigzag, curved, thick, thin.

questions.q: Which is your favorite line and why?
questions.a: Names a line type with a reason, e.g., 'thick zigzag, it looks like lightning.'

weeks.assessment_key: Line sampler: 12 boxes each with a different, correctly labeled line (e.g., straight, curved, zigzag, wavy, spiral, dotted, dashed, thick, thin, broken, vertical, horizontal, diagonal, contour). Reflection names a favorite line with art words. Proficient = 10-12 correct labels + art words; developing = 6-9; beginning = under 6.

weeks.prep: Image of Kandinsky's 'Squares with Concentric Circles' (1913), cut-paper shapes, cups or a compass for tracing, oil pastels, ruler.
misconceptions: Thinking organic shapes are just 'messy': organic shapes are natural, curvy, free-form (leaves, clouds).
Thinking abstract art has no plan: Kandinsky chose colors and shapes carefully to create feelings.

days.guide: Sort cut shapes into geometric and organic; find both at home.

questions.q: Is a leaf geometric or organic?
questions.a: Organic.

questions.q: Is a window pane geometric or organic?
questions.a: Geometric (rectangle).

days.guide: Look at Kandinsky's painting; describe shapes, colors and patterns.

questions.a: Circles inside circles (concentric circles) inside squares.
Art that uses shapes, colors and lines instead of showing real things.

days.guide: Draw a 3x4 grid; fill each square with concentric circles in oil pastel, a different color in each ring.

questions.q: How many squares in a 3x4 grid?

questions.a: Circles inside each other with the same center.

days.guide: Finish the grid; add a border of geometric shapes.

questions.q: What shapes are in your border?
questions.a: Geometric shapes such as triangles, squares, circles.

days.guide: Tell which square you like best using geometric, pattern, contrast.

questions.a: A big difference, like light next to dark or warm next to cool colors.

weeks.assessment_key: Artwork: 3x4 grid (12 squares) with concentric circles in each, varied colors in each ring, border of geometric shapes. Reflection uses 'geometric,' 'pattern,' 'contrast' correctly (e.g., 'I like the square with yellow next to purple because the contrast makes it pop'). Proficient = complete grid + all three words used correctly.

weeks.prep: Images of Matisse's 'The Snail' and 'Icarus' (from his book 'Jazz'), colored paper, scissors, glue sticks, background paper; phone for photos.
misconceptions: Thinking negative space is 'nothing': it is the space around and between shapes, and it can be a shape itself.
Gluing before planning: try several arrangements first.

days.guide: Look at 'The Snail'; explain that when Matisse was ill and used a wheelchair, he 'drew with scissors' by cutting painted paper.

questions.q: How did Matisse make his cut-outs?
questions.a: He cut shapes from paper he had painted with gouache and had them arranged and pinned or glued.

questions.q: Why did Matisse start making cut-outs?
questions.a: After a serious illness he could not stand to paint for long, so he cut paper instead.

days.guide: Practice safe scissor use; cut 10 organic shapes freehand like leaves and seaweed.

questions.a: No, we cut freehand, 'drawing with scissors.'

days.guide: Arrange shapes three ways; photograph each; choose the best.

questions.a: How the parts of an artwork are arranged.

days.guide: Use the leftover paper (negative space) to make a second collage.

questions.a: The shapes themselves (the objects).
The space around and between the shapes.

days.guide: Present both collages; explain the arrangement.

questions.q: Why did you choose this arrangement?
questions.a: Specific reason: balance, contrast, movement.

weeks.assessment_key: Collage: at least 10 freehand organic shapes arranged thoughtfully; second collage uses negative-space leftovers. Explanation names a reason for the chosen arrangement (balance, color contrast, movement). Proficient = both collages + specific reason; developing = one collage or vague reason.

weeks.prep: Image of Mondrian's 'Broadway Boogie Woogie' (1942-43) plus one of his earlier black-line grid paintings; black tape or marker; red, yellow, blue paper; masking tape for hanging; index cards for labels.
misconceptions: Thinking all Mondrian paintings have black lines: 'Broadway Boogie Woogie' uses yellow lines dotted with little red, blue and gray squares, like New York City traffic and jazz music.
Mixing up vertical and horizontal: vertical goes up and down like a flagpole; horizontal goes side to side like the horizon.

days.guide: Compare 'Broadway Boogie Woogie' with Kandinsky's circles; list how each used lines and shapes.

questions.q: How are Mondrian and Kandinsky different?
questions.a: Mondrian used straight vertical/horizontal lines and rectangles; Kandinsky used circles and curves.
New York City (its street grid, lights and jazz).

days.guide: Sketch streets near home as vertical and horizontal lines.

questions.a: Up-and-down lines.
Side-to-side lines.

days.guide: Turn the sketch into Mondrian style: black lines and red, yellow, blue rectangles.

questions.a: Red, yellow and blue.

days.guide: Hang the unit's artworks; label each with title and materials.

questions.a: Title and materials (and artist name).

days.guide: Give a gallery tour naming 5 lines and both kinds of shapes.

questions.q: Point to a geometric and an organic shape.
questions.a: Geometric in Mondrian/Kandinsky work; organic in Matisse collage.

weeks.assessment_key: Mondrian-style artwork: neighborhood streets drawn as vertical and horizontal lines; rectangles filled with red, yellow, blue. Gallery tour names 5 line types (e.g., vertical, horizontal, zigzag, curved, spiral) and both shape kinds (geometric, organic). Labels have title and materials. Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Recordings: Sousa's 'The Stars and Stripes Forever' (march), Strauss's 'The Blue Danube' (waltz); wooden spoons or rhythm sticks; draw a chart of 8 hearts.
misconceptions: Confusing beat and rhythm: beat is the steady pulse; rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds (often the words).
Speeding up: a steady beat stays the same speed.

days.guide: Feel your heartbeat; pat a steady beat to 'The Stars and Stripes Forever.'

questions.q: How is a beat like a heartbeat?
questions.a: Both are steady and keep going evenly.

days.guide: Point to 8 hearts on a beat chart while chanting 'Engine, Engine Number Nine.'

questions.q: How many beats did you point to?
questions.a: 8 (one per heart).

days.guide: Pat the beat while clapping the words of 'Twinkle, Twinkle.'

questions.a: The pattern of long and short sounds, like the words of a song.

questions.q: Which stays even: beat or rhythm?
questions.a: The beat.

days.guide: March to music in 2 (count 1-2); sway to 'The Blue Danube' in 3 (count 1-2-3).

questions.q: Does a waltz feel in 2 or 3?
Does a march feel in 2 or 3?
questions.a: In 2 (1-2, left-right).

days.guide: Keep a steady beat on spoons with 3 songs; explain beat in one sentence.

questions.a: How fast or slow the beat is.

weeks.assessment_key: Steady-beat check: keeps an even beat on spoons through 3 songs without rushing or dragging. One-sentence explanation: 'The beat is the steady pulse that keeps going through the music, like a heartbeat.' Proficient = 3 songs steady + correct sentence.

weeks.prep: Rhythm flash cards (draw quarter notes, eighth-note pairs, quarter rests on index cards), rhythm sticks or pots.
misconceptions: Thinking ti-ti takes two beats: two eighth notes share ONE beat.
Skipping the rest: a rest still takes up a beat in silence.

days.guide: Teach ta (quarter note, 1 sound per beat) and ti-ti (two eighth notes, 2 sounds per beat). Clap 8 cards.

questions.a: One beat (two quick sounds).
Clap, clap-clap (quick), clap, clap.

days.guide: Teach the quarter rest; read patterns with rests; play rhythm echo.

questions.q: What do you do on a quarter rest?
questions.a: Stay silent for one beat.

days.guide: Match food words: pie = ta; apple = ti-ti; watermelon = ti-ti ti-ti. Write 4 food rhythms.

questions.a: Ti-ti.
Two beats (ti-ti ti-ti).

days.guide: Play written rhythms on sticks or pots while keeping the beat.

questions.a: Four quick hits, one hit, one silent beat.

days.guide: Read 6 new rhythms; write 2 for a parent to clap.

questions.q: How many beats must each card have?
questions.a: Four.

weeks.assessment_key: Rhythm reading: claps 6 new 4-beat rhythms correctly (ta = one sound on a beat; ti-ti = two even sounds on one beat; rest = silent beat). Writing: 2 rhythms with exactly 4 beats each that a parent can clap. Proficient = 5-6 correct + 2 correct written rhythms.

weeks.prep: Pots, buckets and wooden spoons; a 'We Will Rock You'-style stomp-stomp-clap beat clip.
misconceptions: Stopping the ostinato when someone else sings: an ostinato keeps repeating underneath.
Improvising longer than 4 beats: answers match the question's length.

days.guide: Learn stomp, pat, clap, snap; echo 10 four-beat patterns.

questions.a: Stomp, pat, clap, snap.

days.guide: Perform a repeated ostinato while a parent sings 'Row, Row, Row Your Boat.'

questions.a: A short pattern repeated over and over.

days.guide: Play two layered rhythms on bucket/pot with a family member.

questions.a: Two or more parts played at the same time.

days.guide: Clap 4-beat 'questions'; child improvises 4-beat 'answers.'

questions.a: Making up music on the spot.

days.guide: Perform the stomp-pat-clap-snap ostinato under a chanted rhyme.

questions.q: What has to stay steady when the parts layer?
questions.a: The beat.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance: plays a steady stomp-pat-clap-snap ostinato under a chanted rhyme without stopping or speeding up. Proficient = steady throughout and pattern repeats correctly; developing = 1-2 slips; beginning = can't keep the pattern.

weeks.prep: Index cards, Chrome Music Lab Rhythm, homemade shaker or pot drum, pencil.
misconceptions: Uneven measures: in 4/4, every measure must have exactly 4 beats.
Thinking bar lines are rests: bar lines just divide the music into measures.

days.guide: Teach bar lines and measures in 4/4 (4 beats per measure). Draw 4 measures.

questions.q: How many beats in each measure of 4/4?

questions.a: Bar lines.

days.guide: Compose a 4-measure piece with ta, ti-ti, rest on cards.

questions.q: Does 'ta ti-ti rest ta' fill one 4/4 measure?
questions.a: Yes: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 beats.

days.guide: Recreate the piece in Chrome Music Lab Rhythm.

questions.q: Did it sound the way you planned?
questions.a: Child compares.

days.guide: Practice on shaker; repeat the trickiest measure slowly.

questions.q: Why practice a tricky measure slowly?
questions.a: To get it correct, then speed up.

days.guide: Perform; explain rhythm choices.

questions.a: How beats are grouped, like in 4s (4/4).

weeks.assessment_key: Notation: 4 measures in 4/4, each with exactly 4 beats of ta, ti-ti and rest, with bar lines and a double bar at the end. Performance steady; explanation gives a reason for rhythm choices. Proficient = all measures correct + steady + reason.

weeks.prep: Red, yellow, blue tempera or watercolor; brushes; paper plates; water cups; paper towels.
misconceptions: Thinking you can mix primaries from other colors: primaries can't be mixed.
Using dirty brushes: wash between colors to keep colors clean.

days.guide: Paint red, yellow and blue blobs; practice brush washing.

questions.a: Red, yellow, blue.

days.guide: Mix orange, green, purple on a plate; record recipes.

questions.a: Green.
Purple.

days.guide: Paint a 6-part color wheel on a plate.

questions.q: What color goes between yellow and blue?
questions.a: Green.

days.guide: Find objects in each wheel color; photograph or draw.

questions.a: Example: an orange, a carrot.

days.guide: Name primary and secondary colors and how to mix each.

questions.a: Orange, green, purple.

weeks.assessment_key: Color wheel order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple (violet), each secondary between its two primaries. Oral: primaries = red, yellow, blue; red + yellow = orange; yellow + blue = green; blue + red = purple. Proficient = all correct.

weeks.prep: Image of Van Gogh's 'The Starry Night' (1889), tempera paints, old magazines, scissors.
misconceptions: Thinking warm colors are just 'hot' colors: they also feel energetic, happy or angry; cool colors feel calm, sad or peaceful.
Thinking Van Gogh painted what he saw exactly: he used swirling, exaggerated brushstrokes to show feeling.

days.guide: Cut and sort 12 magazine pictures into warm and cool piles; describe feelings.

questions.a: Red, orange, yellow.
Blue, green, purple.

days.guide: Look at 'The Starry Night' 3 minutes; use 'I see… I think… I wonder…'.

questions.q: What do you see in 'The Starry Night'?
questions.a: Swirling sky, bright stars, a crescent moon, a small village with a church steeple, a tall dark cypress tree.
Answers vary with reasons: dreamy, exciting, restless, peaceful.

days.guide: Paint a night sky over your house using only cool colors and swirling strokes.

questions.a: The group of colors an artist chooses (or the tray for mixing).

days.guide: Paint a sunset over the same house using only warm colors.

questions.q: What colors are in your sunset?
questions.a: Warm colors: red, orange, yellow.

days.guide: Hang both; explain how the palette changed the mood.

questions.a: Cool = calm, quiet night; warm = bright, energetic sunset.

weeks.assessment_key: Paintings: night painting uses only cool colors with swirling strokes; sunset uses only warm colors. Oral comparison: 'The cool palette makes the house feel calm/quiet/sleepy; the warm palette makes it feel cozy/bright/exciting.' Proficient = both palettes correct + uses warm, cool, mood.

weeks.prep: Image of Monet's 'Water Lilies,' white and black paint, one color, watercolor paper, brushes; a spot outdoors.
misconceptions: Adding too much black for shades: add a tiny dot at a time.
Thinking Impressionists painted every detail: they used short dabs to capture light quickly.

days.guide: Make a 7-step value strip: middle pure color, white added on one side, black on the other.

questions.a: A color plus white (lighter).
A color plus black (darker).

days.guide: Look at Monet's 'Water Lilies'; notice short brushstrokes and many tints of blue and green.

questions.q: What did Monet paint again and again?
questions.a: The water lily pond in his garden at Giverny, France.

questions.q: What art style was Monet part of?
questions.a: Impressionism.

days.guide: Paint outside with short dabbed strokes.

questions.a: To capture real light and color as it changed.

days.guide: Add tints where the sun hits and shades where shadows fall.

questions.a: In shadows.

days.guide: Point to 3 tints and 3 shades; explain mixing.

questions.a: How light or dark a color is.

weeks.assessment_key: Value strip: 7 steps, gradual change: tints (white added) lighter on one side, pure color in middle, shades (black added) darker on the other. Landscape: short dabbed strokes; tints where sun hits, shades in shadow. Reflection points to 3 tints and 3 shades and explains mixing. Proficient = smooth value change + correct identification.

weeks.prep: Paints, watercolor paper, sketchbook; 8 printed or onscreen artwork images showing different moods.
misconceptions: Picking colors without a plan: choose a palette that fits the mood first.
Thinking only color shows mood: lines and shapes help too (jagged = tense, curvy = calm).

days.guide: Choose a mood; sketch a scene; note which colors will show it.

questions.a: Dark cool colors, shades, black, purple.

days.guide: Paint the background with the palette, using tints and shades.

questions.q: How do tints and shades add depth?
questions.a: Lighter areas seem closer or lit; darker areas recede or are in shadow.

days.guide: Add main subject and details with lines and shapes from Unit 1.

questions.a: Matches, e.g., wavy for calm.

days.guide: Family guesses the mood; record guesses and clues.

questions.a: Colors, lines, subjects.

days.guide: Sort 8 artwork images by mood; explain one; say what you'd change.

questions.q: Why did you put this image in 'calm'?
questions.a: Cool colors, soft lines, quiet subject.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = palette, lines and shapes all match the chosen mood; family guesses correctly; sorts 8 images with a clear reason; names a change for next time. 3 = mood mostly clear; 2 = mood unclear or few reasons; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Xylophone, piano app, or 5 glasses with water and a spoon; scarves; 'Frère Jacques' recording.
misconceptions: Confusing high with loud: pitch is high/low; dynamics is loud/soft.
Thinking more water makes a higher pitch in glasses: when tapped, more water makes a LOWER pitch.

days.guide: Play note pairs; hands up for high, on knees for low; compare animal sounds.

questions.q: Is a mouse squeak high or low?
questions.a: High.
How high or low a sound is.

days.guide: Fill 5 glasses with different water levels; tap and order from lowest to highest pitch.

questions.q: Which glass sounds lowest when tapped?
questions.a: The one with the most water.

days.guide: Draw the melody map of 'Twinkle, Twinkle': leap up on the second 'twinkle,' up on 'little,' down on 'star,' then steps down for 'how I wonder what you are.'

questions.q: Does 'how I wonder what you are' go up or down?
questions.a: Down by steps.

days.guide: Move a scarf up and down with 'Frère Jacques'; sing it.

questions.a: The shape a melody makes going up, down or staying the same.

days.guide: Identify high/low in 8 pairs; draw the contour of a parent's melody.

questions.q: If the notes go C-D-E, which way is the contour?
questions.a: Up.

weeks.assessment_key: Pitch check: correctly identifies which note is higher in 8 pairs (goal 7/8). Contour drawing goes up, down, or stays the same matching the parent's melody. Proficient = 7-8 correct + accurate contour.

weeks.prep: Curwen hand-sign chart, paper with a 3-line staff, pennies; song lyrics for 'Rain, Rain, Go Away,' 'Star Light, Star Bright,' 'Ring Around the Rosie.'
misconceptions: Thinking la is between sol and mi: la is just above sol; mi is below sol.
Placing mi in the space under sol: when sol is on a line, mi is on the next line down (a skip), and la is the space just above sol.

days.guide: Sing 'Rain, Rain, Go Away' and 'Star Light, Star Bright' with sol-mi signs.

questions.q: Which is higher, sol or mi?
questions.a: Sol.

days.guide: Add la with 'Ring Around the Rosie'; echo 8 sol-mi-la patterns.

questions.q: Where is la compared to sol?
questions.a: One step higher than sol.

days.guide: Place pennies on a 3-line staff for sol-mi-la; sing them.

questions.q: If sol is on the middle line, where is mi?
questions.a: On the bottom line.
In the space just above sol.

days.guide: Improvise a 4-beat sol-mi-la answer to 'What did you eat today?'.

questions.q: Sing an answer using sol, mi and la.
questions.a: Any 4-beat answer using those pitches, e.g., 'I ate pi-zza' on sol-mi-la-sol.

days.guide: Sing 4 penny-staff patterns; echo 4 with signs.

questions.a: Singing syllables (do, re, mi, sol, la…) for pitches.

weeks.assessment_key: Singing/reading check: sings 4 penny-staff patterns accurately (e.g., sol-mi-sol-la-sol-mi) and echoes 4 patterns with correct hand signs (sol = flat hand, palm toward body; mi = flat hand, palm down; la = relaxed, drooping hand). Proficient = 7-8 of 8 correct.

weeks.prep: Recordings and lyrics: 'De Colores' (Mexico), 'Funga Alafia' (West Africa), 'Sakura Sakura' (Japan), 'Bluebird, Bluebird' (American singing game).
misconceptions: Thinking folk songs have one famous composer: they are passed down through communities.
Thinking verse and refrain are the same: the refrain repeats the same words each time.

days.guide: Learn verse 1 of 'De Colores'; it celebrates the colors of nature in spring (fields, birds, rainbow).

questions.a: Mexico (a Spanish-language folk song).
The many colors of nature in springtime.

days.guide: Learn 'Funga Alafia' with welcoming movements; sing it as a greeting.

questions.a: A West African welcome song; 'alafia' means peace or well-being.

days.guide: Listen to 'Sakura Sakura'; draw cherry blossoms.

questions.a: Cherry blossoms.
Calm, gentle, peaceful.

days.guide: Play 'Bluebird, Bluebird': players make windows with raised arms while the bluebird weaves through.

questions.a: Weaves in and out of the 'windows' (raised arms), then picks a new bluebird.

days.guide: Choose a favorite; practice hard parts; sing it for family with an introduction.

questions.a: A part that repeats with the same words.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance: sings a folk song with mostly correct words and pitch, steady beat; spoken introduction tells where it comes from and why they like it (e.g., 'Sakura is from Japan and is about cherry blossoms; I like its calm melody'). Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Chrome Music Lab Song Maker, staff paper, xylophone or piano app.
misconceptions: Composing with too many notes: a short melody with a clear shape is better.
Ignoring feedback: one 'wish' can make the song better.

days.guide: Make 3 Song Maker melodies: one going up, one going down, one repeating.

questions.q: How does a melody that goes up look on Song Maker?
questions.a: The colored blocks climb higher left to right.

days.guide: Compose an 8-beat melody using sol, mi, la and do; write it.

questions.q: Which is lowest: do, mi, sol or la?
questions.a: Do.

days.guide: Add words about a pet or favorite place.

questions.q: Do your words fit the beats?
questions.a: Each syllable matches a note.

days.guide: Play for a family member; get a star and a wish; revise one part.

questions.q: What is a 'star and a wish'?
questions.a: One thing they liked and one idea to improve.

days.guide: Perform; explain the up/down shape.

questions.a: A short musical sentence.

weeks.assessment_key: Composed melody: 8 beats using do, mi, sol, la, written in staff or iconic notation or recorded; words fit the rhythm; one revision made from a star-and-wish. Explanation of the up/down shape (e.g., 'goes up when the dog jumps'). Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Crayons with paper removed, thin paper, leaves, coins, mesh, bark, scissors, glue.
misconceptions: Thinking all texture can be touched: implied texture only looks like texture (drawn).
Pressing with the crayon tip in rubbings: use the flat side.

days.guide: Touch 10 textures; record words (rough, smooth, bumpy, soft, prickly).

questions.a: Rough, bumpy.

days.guide: Make 12 crayon rubbings; label each.

questions.q: How do you make a rubbing?
questions.a: Paper over a textured surface, rub with the side of a crayon.

days.guide: Cut and arrange rubbings into an animal collage.

questions.a: Bark, carpet, or something with many lines.

days.guide: Draw a pinecone, sweater, rock, feather using lines and dots for texture.

questions.q: How do you show a fuzzy sweater with lines?
questions.a: Short, soft, repeated lines or loops.

days.guide: Explain real vs. implied texture.

questions.a: Texture that is drawn to look like how something feels, but is flat to touch.

weeks.assessment_key: Collage: animal from cut rubbings with textures chosen to suggest fur, scales, etc. Implied texture drawings of pinecone, sweater, rock, feather with lines/dots. Explanation: real texture can be felt; implied texture is drawn to look like how something would feel. Proficient = all + correct explanation.

weeks.prep: Air-dry clay, forks, toothpicks, placemat, water cup; household spheres, cubes, cylinders; paint for later.
misconceptions: Pinching walls too thin or uneven: rotate the pot and pinch evenly.
Attaching a handle without scoring: scratch both surfaces and add a little water (score and slip).

days.guide: Compare flat shapes with forms (ball = sphere, box = cube, can = cylinder); draw a circle and roll a sphere.

questions.q: What is the difference between a circle and a sphere?
questions.a: A circle is flat (2-D); a sphere is a 3-D form like a ball.

questions.q: What form is a soup can?
questions.a: A cylinder.

days.guide: Press a thumb into a clay ball and pinch walls evenly while turning; clean up.

questions.q: How do you make the walls even?
questions.a: Pinch gently while turning the pot.

days.guide: Press textures with forks and toothpicks; add a small animal handle with score and slip.

questions.q: How do you attach clay pieces?
questions.a: Score (scratch) both pieces, add slip or water, press together.

days.guide: When dry, paint a pattern using colors from Unit 3.

questions.a: Wet clay smears and paint won't stick well.

days.guide: Show the pot; describe form, texture and a challenge.

questions.q: Is your pot a shape or a form?
questions.a: A form (3-D).

weeks.assessment_key: Pinch pot: even walls, stable base, pressed texture, small animal handle attached securely, painted pattern. Reflection describes form (3-D, like a bowl or cylinder) and texture and one challenge. Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Image of a Louise Nevelson wall sculpture (e.g., 'Sky Cathedral'); clean recyclables, bottle caps, small boxes, tubes; a shallow box; strong glue; one color of paint (black, white or gold).
misconceptions: Thinking a sculpture must be carved: assemblages are built from found objects.
Thinking one color is boring: one color makes you notice form, light and shadow.

days.guide: Look at a Nevelson wall sculpture; describe how she used wood scraps painted one color.

questions.q: What did Louise Nevelson build her sculptures from?
questions.a: Found wood scraps (furniture parts, crates) arranged in boxes.

questions.q: What color did she often use?
questions.a: Black (also white and gold).

days.guide: Brainstorm 5 ways to turn recyclables into sculpture; sketch.

questions.a: Using something in a new way.

days.guide: Glue boxes, tubes and caps into a shallow box.

questions.a: A sculpture that sticks out from a flat background.

days.guide: Paint the whole sculpture one color; notice shadows.

questions.a: One color.

days.guide: Discuss how one color changed the look and what you repurposed.

questions.q: How did one color change it?
questions.a: Objects blend together; you notice shapes and shadows.

weeks.assessment_key: Relief sculpture: found objects glued into a shallow box, painted one color. Discussion: one color unifies the objects so you see forms and shadows instead of what the objects were; names items repurposed. Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Clay or recyclables, sketchbook, paint.
misconceptions: Planning from only one view: a sculpture is seen from all sides.
Critique means criticize: critique is kind, specific talk about art.

days.guide: Sketch the creature from 2 views; list materials.

questions.a: A sculpture is 3-D and seen from different sides.

days.guide: Build the main form.

questions.a: The biggest basic shape, like the body.

days.guide: Add texture and details; paint.

questions.a: Pressed tools, added materials.

days.guide: Family critique: one like and one question each.

questions.q: Give an example of a kind critique.
questions.a: 'I like the bumpy texture on the back. How did you make the eyes stay on?'

days.guide: Explain texture, form and repurposing in your sculpture.

questions.a: A 3-D shape with height, width and depth.

weeks.assessment_key: Sculpture rubric: 4 = sketch from 2 views, sturdy form, textured details, painted, child explains texture, form and repurposing; 3 = missing one; 2 = missing two; 1 = incomplete. Critique: gives one like and one question.

weeks.prep: Instrument picture cards; orchestra demo videos (BBC Ten Pieces or PBS); rubber bands and a box, straws, paper towel tube; 10 instrument sound clips.
misconceptions: Calling the saxophone or flute 'brass' because they're metal: they're woodwinds.
Thinking the piano is only a string instrument: hammers strike strings, so it's often grouped with percussion/keyboards.

days.guide: Watch an orchestra demo; sort cards into strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion.

questions.a: Strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion.

days.guide: Make a rubber-band guitar, a straw oboe (flatten and snip a straw tip) and a tube trumpet (buzz lips into a tube). Compare.

questions.q: How do brass players make sound?
questions.a: Buzzing their lips into a mouthpiece.
Vibrating strings (plucked or bowed).

days.guide: Listen to 10 clips; name each family.

questions.a: The unique sound quality of an instrument or voice.

days.guide: Research one instrument; draw and label it.

questions.a: Woodwinds.

days.guide: Identify families from sound and pictures (10 items).

questions.a: Percussion.

weeks.assessment_key: 10-item check (example key): violin - strings; cello - strings; harp - strings; flute - woodwinds; clarinet - woodwinds; oboe - woodwinds; trumpet - brass; tuba - brass; French horn - brass; timpani/snare drum - percussion. Proficient = 8+/10.

weeks.prep: Recording of Prokofiev's 'Peter and the Wolf' with narrator; character cards.
misconceptions: Thinking the narrator sings: the narrator speaks the story.
Mixing up oboe (duck) and clarinet (cat): duck = oboe's nasal quacky sound; cat = clarinet's smooth sneaky low notes.

days.guide: Listen to each character's theme.

questions.a: Flute.
Strings.

days.guide: Listen to the full piece; hold up the card when each theme plays.

questions.a: Bassoon.

days.guide: Explain why Prokofiev chose each instrument.

questions.q: Why a flute for the bird?
questions.a: It is high, light and quick like a bird.

questions.q: Why French horns for the wolf?
questions.a: They sound low, dark and scary.

days.guide: Draw your favorite scene; label the instrument.

questions.a: The wolf swallows it (it is still quacking inside at the end).

days.guide: Match 7 themes to characters and instruments.

questions.a: A melody that represents a character.

weeks.assessment_key: 7 themes: Bird - flute; Duck - oboe; Cat - clarinet; Grandfather - bassoon; Wolf - three French horns; Peter - strings; Hunters - woodwinds with timpani and bass drum (gunshots). Labeled drawing names the correct instrument. Proficient = 6-7 correct.

weeks.prep: Saint-Saëns 'Carnival of the Animals' recordings: 'The Elephant,' 'Wild Horses' (Hémiones), 'The Swan,' 'Aquarium'; homemade instruments; paper.
misconceptions: Confusing dynamics with tempo: dynamics = loud/soft; tempo = fast/slow.
Thinking 'piano' means the instrument: in music it also means soft.

days.guide: Teach forte (loud) and piano (soft); sing 'Bingo' changing dynamics on signal.

questions.a: Loud.

questions.q: What does piano mean in music?
questions.a: Soft.

days.guide: Teach allegro (fast) and largo (slow); move to 'The Elephant' and 'Wild Horses.'

questions.a: Slow (like largo).
Very fast (allegro).

days.guide: Listen to 'The Swan' and 'Aquarium'; describe dynamics and tempo.

questions.a: Slow and soft, a smooth cello melody.

days.guide: Play an animal on a homemade instrument; family guesses.

questions.q: How would you play a mouse?
questions.a: Soft and fast, high sounds.

days.guide: Identify dynamics and tempo in 4 excerpts; state preference.

questions.a: Camille Saint-Saëns.

weeks.assessment_key: Listening check (4 excerpts): The Elephant - slow, heavy, fairly loud low double bass; Wild Horses - very fast (allegro/presto), loud, racing pianos; The Swan - slow, soft (piano), smooth cello; Aquarium - medium-slow, soft, shimmering. Preference given with music words. Proficient = 6+ of 8 dynamic/tempo labels correct + reason.

weeks.prep: Recordings: a lullaby, a march, a dance tune, a commercial jingle; paper and paints.
misconceptions: Thinking music is only for listening for fun: music has purposes (sleep, marching, selling, celebrating, worship).
Giving preferences without reasons: use music words (tempo, dynamics, instruments).

days.guide: List all music heard in one day and its purpose.

questions.a: To make shopping pleasant or set a mood.

days.guide: Listen to a lullaby, march, dance tune and jingle; explain how tempo and dynamics fit.

questions.q: Why is a lullaby slow and soft?
questions.a: To calm a baby to sleep.
A short catchy song in an ad to help you remember a product.

days.guide: Interview family about favorite songs; make a playlist.

questions.q: Why does someone in your family like their song?
questions.a: Records their reason.

days.guide: Paint while listening to two contrasting pieces; compare.

questions.q: How did the music change your painting?
questions.a: E.g., fast music made quick jagged strokes.

days.guide: Tell your favorite piece from the unit with music words.

questions.q: Explain your favorite using a music word.
questions.a: Uses tempo, dynamics, timbre or instruments.

weeks.assessment_key: Purpose sort: lullaby - slow, soft, to calm for sleep; march - steady, strong, medium-fast, to move together/parade; dance tune - lively, strong beat, to dance; jingle - short, catchy, to help people remember a product. Proficient = all 4 correct with tempo/dynamics reasons + favorite explained with music words.

weeks.prep: Tissue paper, scissors, string, glue; photos of papel picado.
misconceptions: Cutting on open edges: cut along the folds to make symmetrical holes.
Thinking papel picado is only for one holiday: it's used for many celebrations.

days.guide: Look at papel picado; discuss purposes (Día de los Muertos, weddings, fiestas, holidays).

questions.a: Mexican folk art of cut tissue-paper banners.
Celebrations like Día de los Muertos, weddings, birthdays and holidays.

days.guide: Fold and cut shapes from scrap paper to make symmetrical designs.

questions.a: Both halves match like a mirror image.

days.guide: Fold and cut 4 tissue flags.

questions.a: One cut makes matching shapes on both sides.

days.guide: String the flags into a banner and hang it.

questions.q: Where would you hang your banner?
questions.a: Answer varies.

days.guide: Compare papel picado to family decorations.

questions.a: Both decorate to celebrate special days.

weeks.assessment_key: Banner: 4 folded and cut flags with symmetrical designs strung together. Comparison names how papel picado and family decorations are alike (decorate for celebrations) and different (materials/traditions). Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Rubber fish replica (or a fish from the market), washable tempera and brush, newsprint or rice paper; museum images of gyotaku.
misconceptions: Using thick paint: a thin layer shows scale detail; thick paint blobs.
Thinking gyotaku started as art: it started as a fisherman's record.

days.guide: Learn gyotaku history; look at examples.

questions.a: Fish rubbing (gyo = fish, taku = rubbing).
To record the size of fish they caught.

days.guide: Brush thin paint on the fish; lay paper; rub gently head to tail; make 2 prints and compare.

questions.a: Usually the one with a thinner, even layer of paint.

days.guide: Make 3 more prints with different colors and paper.

questions.q: Which combination showed the most detail?
questions.a: Records observations.

days.guide: Choose the best print; paint in the eye; sign it.

questions.a: The eye doesn't print clearly, so artists paint it in.

days.guide: Write 3 sentences connecting history, art and Unit 5 rubbings.

questions.q: How is gyotaku like a crayon rubbing?
questions.a: Both transfer the real texture of an object onto paper.

weeks.assessment_key: Print: clear fish shape with visible scale texture, eye painted in, signature. Reflection (3 sentences) e.g.: 'Japanese fishermen in the 1800s printed fish to record their size. People saw the prints were beautiful, so gyotaku became an art. Like my rubbings, it shows texture by transferring it onto paper.' Proficient = good detail + all three ideas.

weeks.prep: Construction paper strips, paper loom; images of kente cloth from Ghana; Calisphere photos of Pomo baskets; yarn and rope or pipe cleaners.
misconceptions: Thinking kente colors are random: weavers choose colors for meaning.
Thinking baskets were only decoration: Pomo baskets were used for cooking, storing, carrying, gifts and ceremonies.

days.guide: Look at kente; learn color meanings (gold = wealth/royalty, green = growth/harvest, red = sacrifice/strength, black = maturity/ancestors, blue = peace).

questions.a: Ghana in West Africa.

questions.q: What does green mean in kente?
questions.a: Growth, harvest, renewal.

days.guide: Weave paper strips over-under on a paper loom.

questions.a: Warp: the threads held in place on the loom; weft: the threads woven over and under across them.

days.guide: Look at Pomo baskets; some held water; discuss uses.

questions.q: How could a basket hold water?
questions.a: It was woven so tightly that it was watertight.

questions.q: Name a use for Pomo baskets.
questions.a: Cooking, storage, gathering, gifts, ceremonies.

days.guide: Make a coiled basket with yarn wrapped around rope or pipe cleaner.

questions.a: Wrapping and spiraling a bundle around and around to build a basket.

days.guide: T-chart comparing kente and Pomo baskets; share a similarity.

questions.a: Both are woven, have patterns, and carry cultural meaning.

weeks.assessment_key: Paper weaving: over-under alternating rows, colors chosen with meanings stated. Coiled basket: yarn wrapped and spiraled into a dish. T-chart: Kente - cotton/silk thread, strip-woven on looms in Ghana by Asante and Ewe weavers, bold geometric patterns, worn for special occasions; Pomo baskets - plant fibers (sedge, willow, bulrush), feathers, shell beads, by Pomo weavers of Northern California, used for cooking, storage, gifts and ceremonies. Similarity: both are woven with patterns and carry tradition. Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Photos of Chicano Park murals (San Diego) and the Great Wall of Los Angeles; butcher paper; tempera paints.
misconceptions: Thinking murals are graffiti: murals are planned public artworks, usually with permission and community input.
Thinking public art is only decoration: it tells community stories and history.

days.guide: Look at Chicano Park murals and the Great Wall of Los Angeles; discuss stories and audience.

questions.a: Murals painted on freeway bridge pillars in San Diego celebrating Mexican American (Chicano) history and culture.

questions.q: What is the Great Wall of Los Angeles?
questions.a: A very long mural (about half a mile) led by Judith Baca, painted with young people, showing California history.

days.guide: Find local public art; sketch it; write who might enjoy it.

questions.a: Art in public places that everyone can see.

days.guide: Sketch a mural design about family or community with a pattern border.

questions.q: What story does your mural tell?
questions.a: Child explains.

days.guide: Transfer to butcher paper; paint with a mood palette.

questions.a: An artist who paints murals.

days.guide: Present; explain how public art strengthens a community; name one cultural art form.

questions.q: How does public art help a community?
questions.a: Shares stories and history, brings people together, makes places beautiful.

weeks.assessment_key: Mural presentation: design tells a family/community story with people, places and pattern border, mood palette. Explanation: public art makes a community stronger by sharing its stories and history, bringing people together, and making places beautiful. Names one cultural art form (papel picado, gyotaku, kente, Pomo baskets) and its use. Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Open floor, scarves, masking tape, instrumental music.
misconceptions: Mixing locomotor and nonlocomotor: locomotor travels; nonlocomotor stays in place.
Forgetting middle level: high (tiptoes/reaching), middle (standing/bent), low (near floor).

days.guide: Practice locomotor (walk, skip, gallop, slide) and nonlocomotor (twist, bend, stretch, swing) moves; call them out.

questions.a: Nonlocomotor (stays in place).
Yes, it travels.

days.guide: Freeze in high, middle, low shapes (curved, straight, twisted); make 6 statues.

questions.a: Curled up close to the floor.

days.guide: Tape straight, curved and zigzag pathways; travel each with a different movement.

questions.a: The path your body makes as it travels across the floor.

days.guide: Create movement for a storm, a growing seed, a melting snowman with scarves.

questions.q: How might a melting snowman move?
questions.a: Starts high and slowly sinks to a low level.

days.guide: Perform a 30-second dance with 3 levels, 2 pathways, beginning and ending shapes.

questions.a: High, middle and low.

weeks.assessment_key: Movement checklist for the 30-second dance: beginning shape; uses 3 levels (high, middle, low); 2 pathways (e.g., straight, curved, zigzag); ending shape. Proficient = all 5 items.

weeks.prep: A version of 'The Three Billy Goats Gruff,' simple costume pieces, a chair as the bridge.
misconceptions: Thinking acting is just saying lines: bodies, gestures and voices show character.
Shouting all the troll's lines: change volume and speed to show feeling.

days.guide: Read the story; practice each goat's and the troll's walk, stance and voice.

questions.q: Why do the goats want to cross the bridge?
questions.a: To eat the green grass on the hillside on the other side.

questions.q: How is the little goat's walk different from the big goat's?
questions.a: Little goat: light, quick 'trip-trap'; big goat: heavy, loud stomp.

days.guide: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.

questions.q: What does the smallest goat tell the troll?
questions.a: Wait for my bigger brother; he is much bigger and tastier.

days.guide: Discuss 'what if' choices; choose a new plot idea.

questions.q: How does the original story end?
questions.a: The biggest goat knocks the troll off the bridge into the river, and the goats eat grass and get fat.

days.guide: Act out the original, then the new version.

questions.a: A movement of the body or hands that shows meaning.

days.guide: Share both; tell which choice changed the story most.

questions.a: The events of a story in order.

weeks.assessment_key: Participation rubric: uses different body, gesture and voice for each character; follows the story's plot; contributes a new plot idea and performs the new version. 4 = all with clear choices; 3 = most; 2 = some; 1 = minimal.

weeks.prep: Recording of 'Peter and the Wolf' or 'Carnival of the Animals,' props, homemade percussion.
misconceptions: Thinking the arts work separately: dance, drama and music together tell a richer story.
Rehearsing without fixing anything: fix one problem each run-through.

days.guide: Choose a scene; list characters and events.

questions.q: Who are the characters in your scene?
questions.a: Lists them.

days.guide: Create a movement for each character matching its music (slinky clarinet cat, heavy elephant).

questions.q: How does the cat's music make you move?
questions.a: Sneaky, smooth, slinky steps.

days.guide: Add percussion sound effects and a narrator line for each part.

questions.a: Tells the story to the audience.

days.guide: Rehearse twice, fixing one problem each time.

questions.a: Specific fix.

days.guide: Perform; explain how dance, drama and music worked together.

questions.q: How did the music help the acting?
questions.a: It told the mood and character so movements matched.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric: each character has movement matching its music; sound effects and narrator lines; smooth sequence after rehearsal; explanation of how dance (movement), drama (character/narration) and music (instruments, tempo, dynamics) worked together. 4 = all; 3 = one weak area; 2 = several gaps; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Sketchbook, pastels, watercolor, collage paper; all artwork from the year.
misconceptions: Thinking art about your life must be a big event: everyday moments count.
Using the same material every time: try a different medium.

days.guide: List 5 favorite events this year; sketch two.

questions.a: What the artwork is about.

days.guide: Choose one event; plan using lines, shapes, colors, textures.

questions.q: Which art element will you use to show the mood?
questions.a: Names color, line, etc.

days.guide: Create with mixed media.

questions.a: Art made using more than one material.

days.guide: Create a second piece about a community place using a different material.

questions.a: Names material.

days.guide: Sort all year's artworks into exhibit themes.

questions.q: Which theme fits your Matisse collage?
questions.a: Nature (organic leaf/seaweed shapes) or another logical theme.

weeks.assessment_key: Two artworks about home/community events and places using line, shape, color, texture from earlier units; second piece uses a different material. Theme sort: all year's works grouped into themes like Nature, Me and My Family, Around the World. Proficient = both pieces + logical sort.

weeks.prep: Chrome Music Lab Song Maker, recording device, percussion.
misconceptions: Lyrics that don't fit the beat: clap the words first.
Melodies that jump randomly: use mostly steps with a few leaps.

days.guide: Write 4 short lines about your community.

questions.a: The words of a song.

days.guide: Clap the rhythm of the lyrics; write in ta and ti-ti.

questions.a: Three syllables: e.g., ti-ti ta (two quick then one longer); accept a rhythm that fits how they speak it.

days.guide: Set the words to a sol-mi-la-do melody.

questions.a: Do.

days.guide: Perform; get a star and wish; revise.

questions.a: Specific revision.

days.guide: Record the revised song with a percussion ostinato.

questions.a: A short repeated rhythm, e.g., ta ta ti-ti ta.

weeks.assessment_key: Recorded song: 4 lines of lyrics about community; rhythm written in ta/ti-ti; melody uses sol, mi, la, do; revision from feedback; percussion ostinato added. Proficient = all parts present and steady.

weeks.prep: Construction paper or cardstock for mats, tape, clips, index cards for labels.
misconceptions: Thinking curating is picking favorites only: a curator picks works that fit a theme.
Labels missing information: title, materials, date.

days.guide: Choose 6 artworks for one theme; explain each.

questions.a: To choose and organize artworks for an exhibit.

days.guide: Compare mats, cardstock mounting, clips; mount each.

questions.a: It looks finished and protects the work.

days.guide: Make museum labels: title, materials, date.

questions.a: Title, materials, date (and artist).

days.guide: Write a 3-sentence artist statement.

questions.a: A short writing explaining who you are as an artist and your work.

days.guide: Plan where each piece hangs; sketch a layout.

questions.a: So the exhibit flows and pieces are seen well.

weeks.assessment_key: Six mounted artworks fitting one theme with reasons; labels with title, materials, date; 3-sentence artist statement (who I am as an artist, favorite piece, why/how made). Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Recordings, paper for programs and invitations.
misconceptions: Practicing only from the beginning: practice the tricky spot by itself.
Thinking audiences don't need manners: they listen quietly and clap at the end.

days.guide: Choose 3 pieces; write a program.

questions.a: A list of what will be performed, in order.

days.guide: Rehearse each; mark one tricky spot.

questions.a: Names a measure or line.

days.guide: Perform for family; apply feedback.

questions.a: Specific change.

days.guide: Design invitations with artwork.

questions.a: What, when, where, who.

days.guide: Run the whole showcase start to finish.

questions.a: Listening quietly, not talking, clapping at the end.

weeks.assessment_key: Dress-rehearsal checklist: program lists 3 pieces in order (a folk song, rhythm composition, community song); gallery tour given; tricky spots improved; starts and ends performances clearly (bow). Proficient = all checklist items.

weeks.prep: Home gallery set up, instruments, programs, thank-you note paper.
misconceptions: Thinking growth means everything is perfect: growth is improvement over time.
Forgetting to thank guests: thank-you notes show appreciation.

days.guide: Hang the exhibit; set up performance space.

questions.a: A public display of artwork.

days.guide: Give a gallery tour and perform 3 pieces.

questions.q: What will you tell guests about your favorite piece?
questions.a: Title, materials, idea.

days.guide: Watch a family member's performance with good etiquette.

questions.q: How do you show respect as an audience?
questions.a: Sit quietly, watch, clap at the end.

days.guide: Compare fall and spring artworks using art words.

questions.a: Uses art words: more detail, better color mixing, texture.

days.guide: Write a thank-you note; choose summer goals.

questions.q: What is one art goal and one music goal?
questions.a: Specific goals.

weeks.assessment_key: Showcase: gives a gallery tour using art words and performs 3 pieces. Written reflection compares a fall and spring artwork using art words (e.g., line, color, texture, detail) and states one art and one music summer goal. Proficient = all.
